column4: The section frees a neck; 47:4 places “فَضَرْبَ الرِّقَابِ” beside bonds and a choice of release or ransom, staging the same body, restraint, and release.
“وَفِي الرِّقَابِ” names necks among the recipients of beloved wealth, in the same account of piety that includes patience through hardship.
Its expiation is “فَتَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ مُؤْمِنَةٍ,” a believing neck released, directly matching the section's manumission image.
“وَفِي الرِّقَابِ” makes freeing necks a specified destination for charity, as in the section's account of giving wealth to release the owned.
The section's released neck is funded from wealth; 24:33 tells owners to “فَكَاتِبُوهُمْ” when the enslaved seek a contract and to give them from God's wealth.
The section names an asir as someone to feed; 76:8 includes “أَسِيرًا” among those fed despite the givers' love of food.
Freeing a neck is one of this verse's expiations for a broken oath, alongside feeding or clothing the poor.
For the wrong of zihar, 58:3 requires “فَتَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ” before the spouses touch, making release a concrete act of repair.
The verse speaks of captives and “تُفَادُوهُمْ” while condemning their expulsion, directly activating the section's captive-and-ransom sense.
The section opens a bound neck; this verse says the Messenger removes “الْأَغْلَالَ الَّتِي كَانَتْ عَلَيْهِمْ,” a direct release from shackles.
“We ransomed him with a great sacrifice” makes ransom the substitution that saves a person from death, a parallel to release by payment.
The same closing root named in the section appears in “عَلَيْهِم مُّؤْصَدَةٌ”; here the fire is shut upon the wealth-hoarder.
The extended pillars complete 104:8's sealed-fire image, giving a physical enclosure to the section's closed fire.
The section's dictionary form waṣīd means a threshold or door; 18:18 places the cave sleepers' dog at “بِالْوَصِيدِ.”
The section glosses 90:2's root h-l-l as loosening a knot; Moses asks “وَاحْلُلْ عُقْدَةً مِّن لِّسَانِي,” applying that image to speech.
“كُلُّ نَفْسٍ بِمَا كَسَبَتْ رَهِينَةٌ” makes each soul a pledge held for its deeds, matching the section's dictionary image of unlocking a pledge.
After 76:8–11's feeding and fear of the Day, this verse says they are rewarded for patience, joining the section's feeding, self-restraint, and mercy.
The section says sabr can mean holding one's own self; “وَنَهَى النَّفْسَ عَنِ الْهَوَىٰ” makes that self-restraint explicit.
The section distinguishes restraining oneself from binding another; this verse praises those who “يَكْظِمُونَ الْغَيْظَ” and forgive people.
The section defines denial as covering truth; “وَلَا تَكْتُمُوا الْحَقَّ” names the act of hiding that truth.
“وَتَكْتُمُونَ الْحَقَّ” explicitly pairs truth with concealment, clarifying the section's covering sense of disbelief.
Those who conceal revealed proofs and guidance are condemned, a concrete case of the section's claim that deniers cover truth.
The verse's covenant to disclose scripture and their subsequent concealment matches the section's covered truth, while showing the duty to uncover it.
The messenger clarifies much of scripture that people had concealed, directly opening the section's image of covered truth.
The verse accuses people of displaying some scripture while hiding much, a specific instance of the section's covering of truth.
“كُلُّ امْرِئٍ بِمَا كَسَبَ رَهِينٌ” makes a person a pledge for earned deeds, echoing the section's locked pledge and release vocabulary.
The verse's “رِهَانٌ مَّقْبُوضَةٌ” is a pledge held as security, the very kind of locked pledge the section says can be opened.
This continuation says the givers seek neither payment nor thanks, specifying the selfless motive behind 76:8's feeding of a captive.
The givers fear a frowning, distressful Day, linking the section's compassionate acts to its final judgment and fire.
This verse says God protects them from that day's evil, supplying the saving outcome after 76:8–10's charity and fear.
“لَن تَنَالُوا الْبِرَّ حَتَّىٰ تُنفِقُوا مِمَّا تُحِبُّونَ” gives the same costly generosity that frames freeing and feeding in the section.
The section names the h-d-y family and animal necks; 5:2 joins “الْهَدْيَ” with garlands worn by sacrificial animals, a concrete animal-and-neck meeting.
The section's root f-k-k opens a trapped neck; 98:1 uses “مُّنفَكِّينَ” for those who would not desist or separate from denial until clear proof came.
The withheld wealth will “سَيُطَوَّقُونَ مَا بَخِلُوا بِهِ”; the neck becomes the miser's binding, reversing wealth used to free another.
“مَغْلُولَةً إِلَىٰ عُنُقِكَ” pictures one's own hand bound to one's neck, the section's inverse of freeing another person's neck.
The order “خُذُوهُ فَغُلُّوهُ” turns bodily restraint onto the person who failed the section's ethic of faith and care.
The chain “ذَرْعُهَا سَبْعُونَ ذِرَاعًا” extends 69:30's binding scene into a whole-body confinement; the section likewise moves from a bound neck to the shut fire.
After the binding order in 69:30, this verse gives the failure of belief as its cause, paralleling the section's move from denial to punishment.
After the binding order in 69:30, this verse says he did not urge feeding the poor, directly reversing the section's feeding and mercy.
The verse joins deniers, “الْأَغْلَالُ فِي أَعْنَاقِهِمْ,” and companions of the Fire, gathering the section's bound neck and closed-fire outcome.
“الْأَغْلَالُ فِي أَعْنَاقِهِمْ وَالسَّلَاسِلُ يُسْحَبُونَ” gives the neck, chains, and forced movement that reverse the section's act of release.
Immediately after 76:3's guidance of the way, this verse prepares chains, shackles, and a blazing fire for deniers, reversing guidance's free passage.
“فِي جِيدِهَا حَبْلٌ مِّن مَّسَدٍ” places a rope around a condemned woman's neck, the sharp reversal of freeing a neck.
The verse says no ransom will be taken from the hypocrites and their refuge is fire, reversing the ransom that releases a captive and joining it to the section's fire.
A wall divides two groups and has a door whose inside is mercy and outside punishment, a specific boundary that illuminates the section's closed fire.
This verse exempts the companions of the right from the pledge in 74:38, paralleling the section's division between the saved and the people shut over by fire.
The companions in gardens ask about the condemned, a scene that gives the section's companions of the right a vantage opposite those confined in fire.
This verse identifies the people in 74:40's inquiry as criminals, completing the division between the spared and the punished.
The question “مَا سَلَكَكُمْ فِي سَقَرَ” asks how the criminals reached Saqar, connecting conduct to the section's closed-fire outcome.
The criminals say they did not feed the poor, directly reversing the section's food for the needy and captive.
The criminals say they denied the Day of Judgment, giving a specific denial behind the section's transition from covering signs to fire.
This verse carries 69:30's bound person into the blazing fire, completing the restraint-to-fire sequence that the section closes upon.
After the collars and chains in 40:71, the verse says they are stoked in the Fire, completing the same punishment scene.
Those in the Fire wish to leave but cannot, a specific closed boundary against the section's release from bonds.
When the condemned try to leave the Fire they are returned to it, making the section's shut fire an inescapable confinement.
The verse says each attempt to leave the Fire is followed by return, giving the section's closed fire the concrete limit of no exit.
People are bound together in a narrow place of the Fire, an explicit enclosure joining bonds to the fire that closes in the section.
The Fire's canopies surround its occupants, a covering enclosure that makes visible the section's image of punishment closing around people.
The verse gives the guilty a bed in Hell and coverings above them, a direct image of punishment covering them.
Canopies of fire lie above and beneath the punished, a second explicit enclosure around the inhabitants.
On that Day punishment covers people from above and below, giving a bodily image of the section's “covered” condemned.
The guilty are seen bound together in shackles, a concrete restraint parallel to the section's neck and bond.
Their garments are of tar and fire covers their faces, extending the section's binding image into punishment that covers the body.
The sealed pure drink is a covering that preserves a good gift, a useful counterpoint to the section's seal-like fire that confines its occupants.
The next verse identifies the drink's seal as musk, completing a beneficial seal that contrasts with the section's punishing closure.
The woman locks the doors before inviting Joseph, a specific closed-room scene that contrasts with the section's act of opening a binding.
The doors of the Garden are opened for its people, the direct opposite of the section's fire shut over its occupants.
“Heaven's gates will not be opened” for the arrogant, a specific boundary that mirrors the section's sealed fate.
“فِي الْعُقَدِ” names knots as a source of harm, a specific counter-image to the section's loosening of a knot to release a captive.
This is the guidance immediately preceding 76:4's chains; it recalls the section's two guided ways before the uphill act of release.
The preceding verse calls her the carrier of firewood, which makes the following rope around her neck a punishment tied to her own carrying.
The verse opens the passage cited by the section: a man gathers and counts wealth before the shut fire is described.
The hoarder thinks his wealth will make him immortal, a direct setup for the section's closed fire and its contrast with wealth spent to free others.
The hoarder is cast into Hutama, beginning the fire passage completed by the section's cited shut-fire verses.
The question asks what Hutama is, introducing the punishment whose closure the section draws out.
Hutama is called God's kindled fire, specifying the fire in the section's closed-fire image.
The fire reaches hearts, adding its inward reach to the section's image of a fire that closes around its occupants.
This next verse gives the purpose of untying Moses' tongue-knot: that people understand his speech.
If the neck-freeing expiation in 58:3 is unavailable, this verse prescribes fasting, a specific shift from freeing another to disciplining oneself.
The deeds assigned “فِي عُنُقِهِ” are carried at the person's own neck, extending the section's neck-as-site-of-binding image to accountability.
Believers are told to hold fast to God's rope together; this is a chosen bond that contrasts with the coercive neck-rope the section says should be undone.
The believer's firm handhold “لَا انفِصَامَ لَهَا” is an unbroken chosen bond, a boundary against treating every bond as a captive's restraint.
The section says the w-l-d dictionary form can mean a child or a slave; this verse's serving youths fit that secondary sense, though it does not call them slaves.
This continuation of the wall scene has those outside ask, “Were we not with you?”; the believers answer by naming their delay and doubt, specifying the boundary between the two groups.
The speakers say their hearts are in coverings from the message, a direct image of people covering themselves against guidance.
The verse puts coverings on hearts and deafness in ears so people do not understand, a concrete obstruction of guidance like the section's covered sight.
Coverings on hearts and heaviness in ears block understanding of the recitation, extending the section's image of concealment to hearing.
The verse describes coverings on hearts and deafness in ears after turning away, a specific barrier to guidance that matches the section's closure imagery.
The verse joins sealed hearts and hearing to “غِشَاوَةٌ” over sight, a sensory covering parallel to the section's closure and concealment.
A covering is placed on the sight of one who follows desire, and the verse asks who can guide him; this joins the section's cover and guidance images.
“يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ” gives night as a covering, matching the section's named dictionary sense of night as k-f-r because darkness conceals.
This verse also says night covers day, a repeated Quranic formulation of the covering sense the section assigns to night.
Night is made “لِبَاسًا,” a garment that covers, matching the section's dictionary image of darkness covering what is beneath it.
Night is made “لِبَاسًا,” the same explicit covering image as the section's dictionary sense of night as k-f-r.
The oath by night “إِذَا يَغْشَىٰ” gives the section's darkness-covering sense in a direct verbal image.
The oath by night “إِذَا يَغْشَاهَا” pictures it covering the sun, a specific parallel to the section's night-as-concealment sense.
The verse says night is wrapped over day, a physical covering that makes the section's night-as-k-f-r dictionary sense perceptible.
Joseph and the woman race to the door after the room is locked in 12:23, giving a particular attempted passage through the closed space.
In a plant-growth simile the verse uses “الْكُفَّارَ”; the section notes the k-f-r dictionary sense “farmer,” who covers seed with soil, though the verse's interpretation is disputed.
The section says the w-l-d dictionary form can mean a child or a slave; these serving youths fit the secondary sense, though the verse does not state that they are enslaved.
A fish slips away into the sea from the group's meal at the rock; this resembles the section's gazelle escaping a snare, though this verse does not describe a trap.
The section's root f-k-k is glossed as opening; the verse splits grain and date stone to begin growth, a related opening but not a bound creature's release.
The section lists kāfūr as the sheath around a palm blossom; the verse uses “كَافُورًا” in a drink, though that may be a different intended sense.
The verse says to keep oneself patiently with the humble who call on God, closely matching the section's gloss of sabr as holding one's own self rather than another's neck.
This command to be patient with the Lord's decree and resist the sinner develops the same sabr and self-restraint that the section places beside mercy.
The verse says people's earnings have formed a coating over their hearts, a specific inward covering that develops the section's image of denial as concealment.
Those who covered are themselves screened from their Lord on the Day, directly enacting the section's claim that the coverers are covered.
This next verse says they enter the blazing Fire, completing 83:15's veil with the punishment that the section closes over its occupants.
A guilty person wishes to ransom himself from that Day's punishment with his children, reversing a ransom that frees a captive and showing that this release has a limit.
This continuation adds a spouse and brother to the family the guilty person would offer as ransom, widening the contrast with the section's actual release of a captive.
The imagined ransom expands to the clan that shelters him, carrying 70:11's impossible substitution into the social group.
He would offer everyone on earth to ransom himself, completing the escalating but unavailable release in 70:11–13.
The verse identifies the punishment as a blazing flame, specifying what the impossible ransom in 70:11 would avert.
This verse names the companions of the right, repeating the section's category for those whose acts include release and mercy.
This verse names the companions of the left, the opposing group that the section places under its closed Fire.
The passage again introduces the companions of the left, now as the people facing the punishment described in the following verses.
Their punishment begins with scorching wind and boiling water, specific torment that expands the section's closed-fire scene.
The left side has a shade of black smoke, a covering that turns the section's image of covering into punishment.
The smoke is neither cool nor beneficial, specifying the hostile cover over the people of the left.
The verse says they had lived in luxury, a concrete link between unspent abundance and the section's rich man boasting of amassed wealth.
Their persistence in great sin explains why this group receives the punishment contrasted with the section's patient and merciful believers.
They deny being raised after death, the same objection about becoming dust that the section cites with the neck-bound deniers in 13:5.
The next verse extends that denial to their forefathers, completing the resurrection objection begun in 56:47.
Before the shackle order cited in 69:30, this verse gives a person his record in the right hand, the favorable side opposite the bound condemned person.
The right-handed person says he expected to meet his account, giving the favorable side an explicit stance toward judgment.
The right-handed person's outcome is a pleasing life, the counterpart to the fire and bonds described later in the same passage.
The passage places that person in a high garden, completing the favorable outcome opposed to the closed Fire.
Its fruit hangs near, a concrete detail of the ease given to the right-handed person before the passage turns to the left-handed one.
They are told to eat and drink for what they sent ahead, linking deeds to the favorable judgment that contrasts with the section's bound deniers.
The next person receives his record in the left hand and regrets it, directly continuing the division between the section's right and left companions.
He wishes he had never received his record, specifying his rejection of the reckoning that the right-handed person welcomed.
He wishes death had ended everything, continuing his regret before the binding order in 69:30.
He says his wealth did not benefit him, a direct reversal of the section's wealthy man's boast and a lead into the punishment that follows.
He says his authority is gone, completing the loss of power immediately before the order to shackle him.
The person given his record in his right hand receives the favorable side of the judgment, a repeated formulation of the section's division by right and left.
This verse promises an easy reckoning to the right-handed person, specifying the judgment on the released side.
He returns to his family joyful, completing the right-handed outcome before the passage turns to the person given his record behind his back.
The other person receives his record behind his back, the sharp counterpart to the favorable right hand and the section's right/left division.
He calls for destruction, continuing the regret of the person facing the section's closed-fire outcome.
The person enters a blazing Fire, stating the punishment on the side opposite the section's companions of the right.
He had been joyful among his family, a concrete account of his former ease before the judgment described here.
He thought he would never return to God, directly paralleling the section's denial of resurrection before punishment.
The verse says his Lord was watching him, answering the section's question about the person who thinks no one sees him.
The verse rebukes failure to honor the orphan, directly reversing the section's orphan-care and mercy among the acts that pass the obstacle.
It rebukes failure to urge feeding the poor, the direct opposite of the section's feeding in hunger and care for the needy.
The next charge is devouring inheritance greedily, specifying how abundance is consumed instead of used to free and feed others.
The verse names intense love of wealth, a direct counterpoint to the section's spending wealth to release a neck.
Hell is brought forth after the charges about the orphan, poor, and wealth, joining those failures to the section's closed Fire.
The person regrets not sending good ahead for his afterlife, clarifying the lost use of wealth and action before Hell appears.
The next verse says no one punishes as God does, sharpening the judgment that leads directly to the binding in 89:26.
No one binds as God binds, a direct reversal of the section's freeing of a neck and a specific bond at the end of the orphan-and-wealth passage.
The verse links denial of judgment to the conduct that follows, setting up a direct contrast with the section's faith and mercy.
The denier repulses the orphan, a specific opposite to the section's care for the orphan as part of the uphill act.
He does not urge feeding the poor, directly reversing the food and compassion that define the section's charitable scene.
The verse says Hell encompasses the disbelievers, a specific image of the fire surrounding those whom the section says are shut over by it.
When the Quran is recited, a hidden barrier is placed between the reciter and those who do not believe in the Hereafter, a specific obstruction of guidance.
The verse explicitly discusses taking captives and the desire for ransom, giving the section's captive-and-ransom vocabulary a wartime boundary.
The Prophet addresses captives in his hands and promises them better than what was taken from them and forgiveness, a specific continuation of the captive scene.
The verse tests believers with game within reach of their hands and spears; this recalls the section's gazelle in a snare, although it does not say the game was trapped or escaped.
